title: The ledger and the promise
paragraphs: Imagine a public collection whose most disputed object is a small carved box. Its acquisition ledger contains a date, a collector’s signature and a single word: gift. Decades later, a community association requests its return. The collection’s trustees reply that the entry establishes a lawful transfer; the association answers that the circumstances of dispossession make the word gift impossible to accept at face value. Neither party disputes that the box has been carefully conserved. What they dispute is whether careful possession can supply the permission that the original record does not describe. The ledger is therefore indispensable, but it cannot carry every conclusion placed upon it.

The first difficulty is evidentiary. A signature records that somebody endorsed a transaction, yet it does not by itself identify whose authority that person possessed. Nor does an absent objection establish that everyone concerned consented. Silence may reflect agreement, but it may also reflect distance, fear or a record-keeping system that did not preserve dissent. The transfer, be it a gift or a sale, still requires an account of who could authorise it. Calling the ledger incomplete is not equivalent to proving theft. It is a reason to distinguish what the document attests from what the institution has subsequently inferred.

The second difficulty concerns entitlement. An object may have passed through several hands, each receiving assurances from the previous holder. Repetition can make a claim look settled without adding an independent basis for it. A contemporary institution may therefore inherit both a valuable collection and a responsibility to investigate the conditions under which it was assembled. That responsibility need not presuppose that every request succeeds. It does mean that an institution cannot treat its own earlier description as a neutral verdict merely because the description has been reproduced for many years. An inherited statement remains a statement requiring reasons.

Some trustees respond by appealing to stewardship. The collection has paid for conservation, trained specialists and enabled public study; a return, they suggest, would put those achievements at risk. These considerations are relevant to planning the future of an object. They do not automatically settle who may make that plan. Custodianship describes a relationship of care, whereas ownership is a claim to authority over the cared-for thing. Conflating them would allow any sufficiently diligent holder to manufacture an entitlement through continued possession. A promise to conserve can be sincere and valuable while leaving the underlying question of permission unresolved.

The association’s language also deserves scrutiny. It describes the box as inalienable: something no individual could rightfully surrender on behalf of the whole community. That claim may challenge the collector’s signature more fundamentally than an allegation of inadequate payment would. Yet the institution still needs to understand who now speaks for the relevant community, how internal disagreement is represented and what return would entail. Asking those questions need not be a device for postponement. Refusing to ask them could replace one unexamined representative with another. Respect for a claimant involves taking its institutions seriously enough to understand how they make decisions.

One proposal is to submit the matter to a panel empowered to adjudicate the competing claims. A claim that has been adjudicated acquires a different procedural status, but a decision cannot erase every moral question about the procedure that produced it. Jurisdiction matters: which rules apply, who may give evidence and what remedies the panel can order will shape the result. An institution should explain those limits, if only to prevent a narrow decision from being presented as universal vindication. Equally, a claimant’s refusal of a particular forum does not by itself demonstrate that the underlying request lacks substance.

Restitution is often discussed as though it were simply conservation in reverse: the box leaves the institution and the problem disappears. Repatriation, however, may require agreements about transport, access, future loans and the preservation of records. There may also be disagreements about the destination itself. These practical issues are not reasons to presume that return is impossible. They are reasons to specify the commitments that would make it workable. If shared custody is proposed instead, the parties should state which powers are shared and which remain unequal. An attractive phrase is not a substitute for an allocation of responsibility.

It is also possible to acknowledge a wrong without agreeing immediately on the appropriate form of redress. A public correction of the acquisition record may matter even when negotiations about the object continue. Such a correction should not be advertised as a complete remedy, nor dismissed as worthless because it is incomplete. The institution should preserve the disputed wording alongside the reasons for revising it, if only to show how its earlier certainty was constructed. A revised record can make future decisions more accountable without pretending that improved language has already repaired a material loss.

The strongest conclusion available may thus be deliberately defeasible: the current evidence supports a particular course of action, subject to revision when relevant evidence or legitimate representation changes. This is not an invitation to suspend action indefinitely. A decision can be provisional in its justification and concrete in its consequences. What matters is that the parties identify which uncertainties remain, who bears the cost of delay and what would count as a reason to reconsider. The ledger supplies a starting point for that work. The promise is to avoid turning an inherited label into the last word.
translation: 设想一个公共收藏机构，争议最大的藏品是一只小雕花盒。入藏账册只写着日期、收藏者签名和“赠与”一词。数十年后，一个社区协会要求归还。受托人说这足以证明合法转让；协会则说，财产被剥夺的背景使人无法照字面接受“赠与”。双方都认可盒子保存得很好，争论的是：悉心保管能否补上原记录未说明的许可。账册不可或缺，却承载不了被加在其上的所有结论。
第一个困难在于证据。签名记录某人认可过交易，本身却不能说明此人拥有谁的授权。没有异议记录也不等于所有相关者同意。沉默可能源于赞同，也可能源于距离、恐惧，或不保留反对意见的记录制度。这次转移无论是赠与还是出售，都仍需说明谁有权授权。说账册不完整不等于证明发生盗窃，而是要求区分文献实际证明的内容和机构后来的推断。
第二个困难是权利根据。物品可能辗转多人，每个人都接受了前一位持有者的保证。重复会让主张显得已成定论，却未增加独立依据。今天的机构可能既继承珍贵收藏，也继承调查形成条件的责任。这不预设每项申请都成功，却意味着不能仅因旧描述被重复多年，就把自己的先前说法当中立裁决。继承来的陈述仍需理由支持。
部分受托人诉诸负责任的管理：机构支付修复费用、培养专家、开放研究，归还可能危及这些成果。这些因素关系到藏品未来如何安排，却不能自动决定谁有权安排。保管职责描述照护关系，所有权则主张对被照护之物的支配权限。混同两者，便会使任何足够勤勉的持有者都能靠持续占有制造权利。保存承诺可以真诚而有价值，许可问题仍未解决。
协会的措辞也需审视。它称盒子为不可转让之物，即任何个人都无权代表整个社区让渡。与付款不足的指控相比，这可能更根本地挑战收藏者的签名。但机构仍需了解，如今谁代表有关社区、内部异议如何体现，以及归还具体意味着什么。提出这些问题未必是拖延；不问反而可能以另一位未经检验的代表取代旧代表。尊重申请者，也包括认真理解其决策机构。
一个方案是交由有权裁决竞争主张的委员会处理。经裁决的主张在程序上有了不同地位，决定却无法消除对该程序本身的所有道德质疑。管辖权限很重要：适用规则、谁能举证、可命令何种补救，都会影响结果。机构应说明这些限制，至少避免把狭窄决定说成全面洗清责任。同样，申请者拒绝某个论坛，本身也不能证明请求缺乏实质根据。
归还有时被谈得仿佛只是反向的保存：盒子离馆，问题就消失。然而送回原属地可能涉及运输、访问、未来借展和档案保存的协议，甚至目的地本身也有争议。这些实际问题不能证明归还不可能，而是要求明确使归还可行的承诺。若改提共同保管，就应说明共享哪些权力、哪些仍不平等。动听的词组不能取代责任分配。
承认不当也可能先于就补救方式达成一致。即使实物谈判继续，公开纠正入藏记录仍可能有意义。不能把它宣传成完整补救，也不应因其不完整而说它毫无价值。机构应把有争议的旧措辞和修订理由一并保留，至少显示先前的确定性如何被建构。修订记录可以让后续决策更可追责，却不必假装语言改善已修复实质损失。
因此，最有力的结论或许刻意保留可被推翻性：现有证据支持某种行动，但相关证据或合法代表情况变化时应修订。这不是无限期搁置行动。决定的理由可以暂定，后果仍可以具体。关键是说明还存在哪些不确定、谁承担拖延代价、何种情况构成重审理由。账册提供工作的起点；承诺则是避免让继承来的标签成为最终定论。

grammar.surface: be it a gift or a sale

questions.prompt: Which claim best captures the author’s overall position?
options: An inherited acquisition label should be replaced by automatic return in every case.
Careful conservation independently establishes authority to retain an object.
Acquisition claims require accountable examination of evidence, authority and remedy.
questions.explanation: Across the essay, neither conservation nor a single inherited label settles the matter; the author also scrutinises claimant representation and practical remedies.

questions.prompt: Why does the essay distinguish custodianship from ownership?
options: To reject conservation as a useful activity.
To show that care does not by itself supply permission or entitlement.
To establish that all careful holders act without consent.
questions.explanation: Paragraph four accepts conservation as relevant and valuable, but denies that diligence alone can manufacture an entitlement.

questions.prompt: In the final paragraph, what does “defeasible” imply?
options: Open to justified revision if relevant conditions change.
So uncertain that no action may ever follow.
Legally binding in every possible jurisdiction.
questions.explanation: The author immediately specifies revision when evidence or legitimate representation changes, while explicitly rejecting indefinite inaction.

questions.prompt: What is the role of “if only to prevent a narrow decision from being presented as universal vindication”?
options: It states that the panel can resolve every moral question.
It asserts that explaining limits has exactly one possible benefit.
It offers a sufficient limited reason for explaining procedural limits.
questions.explanation: Paragraph six treats avoiding overstatement as a worthwhile minimum rationale, without claiming exhaustive benefits or universal moral resolution.

questions.prompt: Why does the author question how the association represents its community?
options: To dismiss the request whenever any internal disagreement exists.
To apply scrutiny to present representation as well as past authorisation.
To show that only the trustees can speak about the box.
questions.explanation: Paragraph five warns against replacing one unexamined representative with another, while also saying inquiry need not be a delaying tactic.

notes: 这是虚构情境中的语言与论证练习，不陈述任何特定法律辖区的实际法律结论。
关注作者分别限制机构与申请者的主张，并区分证据、权限、程序和补救。
